versions.text:
For sixty years the Ferrin loaf, a dark rye so coarse that the grain showed in every slice, had come from one oven in Tollin. Nell Ferrin had baked it first, and before she died she made her granddaughter Ada promise to keep it exactly as it was. It sat on the shelf by the window at four pennies. Orla Penn, the shop's oldest customer, bought one every morning, and Hob Tasker, the innkeeper, took two dozen a day for the Grey Hen, three dozen on Saturdays.

The rye was ground by Brann Cole, the miller below the town, and in October his great stone cracked. A new one could come from the quarry in spring. Until then Brann could grind only a finer flour on his small stone, though twenty sacks of coarse rye, about six weeks of loaves, stood already ground in his loft.

Joss, Ada's nephew and apprentice, carried Nell's old hand mill up from the cellar and tried it; grinding rye for a single batch took him the whole night, longer than the baking itself. It was Ada's sister Merry, writing from Dunmere over the ridge, who suggested the answer: the big mill there sold coarse rye at a higher price, and the Tuesday carter would bring it across for a fee.

Ada wrote back the same day; a few pennies more seemed a small price for keeping her promise. When the first sacks came over the ridge, she stood at the counter to break the first loaf in two and study the crumb. It was right, and Orla said it tasted exactly as Nell's had. The loaf was on the shelf every morning that winter, but Ada chalked a new figure on the board by the door, and Hob grumbled as he paid.

The whole of Tollin's rye now came on one cart, over one high, bare road, and Brann's twenty sacks would cover six weeks at most if that road closed. Every Tuesday became a wager against the sky. By December Ada was at the shop window an hour before the cart could be due, and it is hard to watch her there without glancing at the clouds; the deep snows that shut the pass most years were still to come.

Ada's sister Merry wrote that the big mill at Dunmere, over the ridge, sold coarse rye at a higher price. It was Orla Penn who told Ada to wait: better an empty shelf until spring, she said, than a loaf that was only nearly Nell's.

Ada took her advice. Her note to Merry gave the reason: a loaf that was nearly Nell's was not the one she had promised. She baked Brann's twenty sacks into a last six weeks of loaves and then took the rye loaf off the shelf until the new stone came. She had to break the news to Hob, who bought the Grey Hen's bread from a baker in Dunmere until spring. Through the winter the shop window held white loaves and wheat buns.

The new stone reached Brann's mill in the second week of April. He set it on a Monday, and Ada baked Nell's loaf again on the Wednesday. It went back on the board by the door at four pennies, and Orla Penn said it tasted the same as before. The shop's daybook shows the gap: rye until December, white bread until April, then rye again.

Ada's sister Merry wrote that the big mill at Dunmere, over the ridge, sold coarse rye at a higher price. It was Brann who talked Ada round: a loaf of his finer flour, he said, would rise better, and nobody would mind.

Ada agreed within the hour, though it meant she would break her word to Nell. The new loaf stood taller and cut cleaner, and it was on the shelf every morning that winter, still sold at four pennies. Orla Penn chewed her first slice for a long while and said it tasted very nice, and after that she bought it on Saturdays only.

So a loaf that had come through sixty years and Nell's own lean winters was given up in an afternoon, to spare Ada a cart and a few pennies. Coarse rye could be had in Dunmere all along, and twenty sacks of it sat in Brann's loft. Ada had weighed her grandmother's bread against a little trouble, and chosen to sell Tollin a loaf that tasted like any town's.

Ada's sister Merry wrote that the big mill at Dunmere, over the ridge, sold coarse rye at a higher price. It was Joss who said what to do: if he and Ada took turns at the handle, the two of them could grind it all.

They used Brann's twenty sacks first, and in late November they began. Each night the two of them ground in turns, often still at the handle before the day could break, and the loaves reached the shelf hours later than they used to. Orla said they tasted exactly as Nell's had, and they were still sold at four pennies.

All winter the two of them fed the shop that way, through frost and short grey days. When the new stone came in spring, Ada could say what few bakers ever can: every loaf she had sold was the one she had promised Nell, kept so by two pairs of hands. It was hard, plain, faithful work, and Tollin ate the better for it.

Ada's sister Merry wrote that the big mill at Dunmere, over the ridge, sold coarse rye at a higher price. It was Hob Tasker who saw a way: baked only for the Saturday market, Brann's twenty sacks would last until spring.

Ada took the plan gladly, since it kept the loaf exactly as Nell had made it; on which days it was baked, Nell had happily said nothing. From then on the rye loaf went into the oven on Friday nights alone, and on Saturdays the line for it ran across the square. It was still sold at four pennies, and Orla said it tasted exactly as Nell's had. By the first snows of winter the Saturday sales would regularly break ten dozen.

The one person in Tollin who suffered by the plan was the man who had thought of it. The Grey Hen's three dozen now had to be bought from the back of a queue that formed at dawn, and Hob spent his Saturday mornings stamping in the cold behind his own customers, while his cook asked daily how the clever idea was getting on, and Ada, ever exact, served him in his turn.
